findings.message: A different agent (Claude) checked the work in a separate headless process.

I found no blocking defects. The dispatcher now checks each asset with claudeAssetMatches. A skill passes if its bytes match exactly, or if its YAML front matter means the same thing and its body bytes match exactly. Any other change, or front matter that can't be parsed, makes verifyPlugin treat the plugin as damaged. The tests run the real dispatcher and profile observer against a copied plugin cache. They separate a header that was only reformatted (accepted, with proof recorded) from changed metadata, a changed body, a changed runtime file and malformed or duplicate keys (each rejected: PreToolUse asks for approval and no proof is written). So the checks fail if semantic matching is missing or too loose. A diagnostic or integrity error still produces the damaged-plugin response, so prompts keep working. The remaining concerns are policy or hardening questions, not failures in the shipped behavior.

The integrity check only guards against accidental corruption, and that is what the comment at mainUnsafe says. inventory.json and identity.json live in the same plugin root they describe, so anyone who can write there can reseal edited skill metadata or runtime files. Adding skill_sha256 doesn't weaken this, but docs and status output should not present the check as tamper-proof.

Semantic skill matching parses YAML 1.2 core with this project's yaml library. If Claude's own front-matter parser reads some construct differently (for example `1.0` vs `1`, YAML 1.1 booleans like `yes`, or merge keys), two headers this check treats as equal could act differently in the host. The ledger defers this as a policy question. It doesn't matter for the skills shipped today, but it could start to matter if skill headers use less common YAML.

The profile observer test includes an `allowed-tools: Bash` addition, which is the metadata change most likely to grant extra privileges. The dispatcher's mutation table doesn't. The semantic hash should reject it the same way, but adding that case to dispatch.test.ts would make sure the dispatcher path covers a permission-widening edit.

The header regex in asset-integrity.ts ends the front matter lazily at the first line that is just `---`. A block scalar whose content contains a bare `---` line would be split early, and that file could never verify semantically. It would still verify on exact bytes. Such a file would be rejected, never wrongly accepted, so this is a false-positive risk only.
Refactor item R2 is still unchecked in the ledger, but verifyInventoryAsset already computes the diagnostic digest only when validation fails. The ledger may just be out of date.
